concepts: Orthogonal matrices and the condition $A^TA=kI$
questions.question: The total number of matrices $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&2y&1\\2x&y&-1\\2x&-y&1\end{pmatrix}$, $(x,y\in\mathbb R,\ x\neq y)$, for which $A^TA=3I_3$, is:
questions.key_idea: $A^TA=3I$ says the columns are mutually orthogonal, each of squared length $3$; only the diagonal gives conditions.
solution: Multiplying out gives $\begin{pmatrix}8x^2&0&0\\0&6y^2&0\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix}$; all off-diagonal entries are $0$ automatically.
$x=\pm\sqrt{\dfrac38},\ y=\pm\sqrt{\dfrac12}$; here $x^2=\tfrac38\neq\tfrac12=y^2$, so $x\neq y$ holds for every choice of signs.

alternate_solutions.idea: For a square matrix $A^TA=3I$ is equivalent to $AA^T=3I$, so use the rows instead of the columns.
solution: $A^TA=3I\Rightarrow A^{-1}=\tfrac13A^T\Rightarrow AA^T=3I$ as well, so the rows of $A$ are orthogonal with squared length $3$.
Row 3 gives the same equation as row 2 ($4x^2+y^2+1=3$).
The remaining conditions are consistent: $R_1\cdot R_2=2y^2-1=0$, $R_1\cdot R_3=-2y^2+1=0$ and $R_2\cdot R_3=4x^2-y^2-1=\tfrac32-\tfrac12-1=0$.
So $x^2=\tfrac38,\ y^2=\tfrac12$ with independent signs: $4$ matrices. Same answer (also $|A|=-12xy$ and $|A|^2=144\cdot\tfrac38\cdot\tfrac12=27=3^3$ agrees).

useful_results: For a square matrix, $A^TA=kI\iff AA^T=kI$ (then $A/\sqrt k$ is orthogonal): both the rows and the columns are mutually perpendicular with squared length $k$.
$A^TA=kI_n\Rightarrow|A|^2=k^n$; here $|A|^2=27$ (and indeed $|A|=-12xy$, $144x^2y^2=27$).
The diagonal of $A^TA$ holds the squared lengths of the columns and the off-diagonal entries are the pairwise dot products; check which off-diagonals vanish identically before solving.
Each independent sign choice of the free parameters multiplies the count by $2$ (here $x=\pm$, $y=\pm$).

concepts: Determinant properties: scalar multiples of rows and columns
questions.question: Let $A=[a_{ij}]$ and $B=[b_{ij}]$ be two $3\times3$ real matrices such that $b_{ij}=(3)^{(i+j-2)}a_{ji}$, where $i,j=1,2,3$. If the determinant of $B$ is $81$, then the determinant of $A$ is:
questions.key_idea: $b_{ij}=3^{i-1}3^{j-1}a_{ji}$ multiplies row $i$ and column $j$ of $A^T$ by powers of $3$, so $|B|=3^{6}|A|$.
solution: Take $3^0,3^1,3^2$ out of rows $1,2,3$ and then $3^0,3^1,3^2$ out of columns $1,2,3$: the common factor is $3^{0+1+2}\cdot3^{0+1+2}=3^6$.
useful_results: If $b_{ij}=u_iv_j\,a_{ij}$ (a rank-one rescaling) then $B=\operatorname{diag}(u)\,A\,\operatorname{diag}(v)$ and $|B|=\prod u_i\prod v_j\,|A|$.
$|A^T|=|A|$, so the transpose built into $a_{ji}$ does not change the determinant.
For an $n\times n$ matrix, $|kA|=k^n|A|$; the pattern $b_{ij}=k^{i+j-2}a_{ij}$ gives $|B|=k^{n(n-1)}|A|$ (here $k^6$ for $n=3$).

concepts: Homogeneous linear systems: non-trivial solutions on the unit sphere
questions.question: Let $A=\{X=(x,y,z)^T: PX=0 \text{ and } x^2+y^2+z^2=1\}$, where $P=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\-2&3&-4\\1&9&-1\end{pmatrix}$, then the set $A$:
questions.key_idea: $|P|=0$ with rank $2$ makes the solutions of $PX=0$ a line through the origin; a line meets the unit sphere in exactly two points.
solution: Put $z=\lambda$: from the first, $x+2y=-\lambda$; from the third, $x+9y=\lambda$.

Then $x=-\lambda-2y=-\dfrac{11\lambda}7$, so $(x,y,z)=\left(-\dfrac{11\lambda}7,\dfrac{2\lambda}7,\lambda\right)$ (it satisfies the second equation too: $\tfrac{22\lambda}7+\tfrac{6\lambda}7-4\lambda=0$).
Two values of $\lambda$ give two points, so $A$ has exactly two elements.

alternate_solutions.idea: The null space is the line along the cross product of two independent rows of $P$; normalise it to get both unit vectors.
solution: Rows $r_1=(1,2,1)$ and $r_3=(1,9,-1)$ are independent, and $|P|=0$ means $r_2$ lies in their span, so the solution set of $PX=0$ is the line perpendicular to both $r_1,r_3$.
Exactly two unit vectors $\pm\dfrac{(-11,2,7)}{\sqrt{174}}$. Same answer.

useful_results: For a $3\times3$ homogeneous system of rank $2$ the solution set is a line through the origin, spanned by the cross product of any two independent rows.
A line through the origin meets the unit sphere $|X|=1$ in exactly $2$ points; rank $3$ gives $0$ points (only $X=0$); rank $1$ (a plane) gives infinitely many (a circle).
Rank-$2$ test for $|P|=0$: if two rows are independent and the third row is a combination of them, the cross product of the two gives the kernel direction.
Counting rule: number of unit solutions $=2$ if nullity is $1$, $\infty$ if nullity is $\ge2$, $0$ if nullity is $0$.

concepts: Powers of a matrix
questions.question: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}x&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$, $x\in\mathbb R$ and $A^4=[a_{ij}]$. If $a_{11}=109$, then $a_{22}$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Square twice: the entries of $A^4$ depend only on $x^2$, so $a_{11}=109$ fixes $x^2=9$.
solution: $A^4=\begin{bmatrix}(x^2+1)^2+x^2&x(x^2+1)+x\\x(x^2+1)+x&x^2+1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}109&a_{12}\\a_{21}&a_{22}\end{bmatrix}$ (the PDF leaves the off-diagonal entries blank).

alternate_solutions.idea: $A^2=xA+I$ (Cayley-Hamilton), so every power is a combination of $A$ and $I$.

useful_results: Cayley-Hamilton for a $2\times2$ matrix: $A^2=(\operatorname{tr}A)A-(\det A)I$; every higher power reduces to $pA+qI$, so $A^n=p_nA+q_nI$ with a Fibonacci-type recurrence.

For $A=\begin{bmatrix}x&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$: $A^n=\begin{bmatrix}F_{n+1}&F_n\\F_n&F_{n-1}\end{bmatrix}$ where $F_{n+1}=xF_n+F_{n-1}$ (Fibonacci polynomials); at $x=1$ these are the Fibonacci numbers.
Squaring twice ($A^4=(A^2)^2$) is faster than multiplying four times, and for a symmetric $A$ all powers stay symmetric.

concepts: Adjoint of a matrix and determinant of adj(adj A)
questions.question: Let $A$ be a $3\times3$ matrix such that $\operatorname{adj}A=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1&1\\-1&0&2\\1&-2&-1\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)$. If $|A|=\lambda$ and $|(B^{-1})^T|=\mu$, then the ordered pair $(|\lambda|,\mu)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: For an $n\times n$ matrix $|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{n-1}$ and $|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)|=|A|^{(n-1)^2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: For $n=3$, $\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)=|A|\,A$, so $B$ is just a scalar multiple of $A$.
solution: $|\operatorname{adj}A|=\lambda^2=9$ (computed from the given matrix), so $|\lambda|=3$ and $\lambda^4=81$.

useful_results: $|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{n-1}$, $\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)=|A|^{n-2}A$, $|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)|=|A|^{(n-1)^2}$ (for invertible $A$).
If only $\operatorname{adj}A$ is given, $|A|$ is known up to sign: $|A|=\pm\sqrt{|\operatorname{adj}A|}$ for $n=3$; the options usually ask for $|\lambda|$ or an even power for this reason.
Check: $A=2I_3$ has $|A|=8$, $\operatorname{adj}A=4I$, $|\operatorname{adj}A|=64=8^2$, $\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)=16I=8\cdot2I$.

concepts: Powers of a matrix with trigonometric entries
questions.question: If $A=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&i\sin\theta\\i\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}$, $\left(\theta=\dfrac\pi{24}\right)$ and $A^5=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}$, where $i=\sqrt{-1}$, then which one of the following is not true?
questions.key_idea: Each multiplication by $A$ adds $\theta$: $A^n=\begin{bmatrix}\cos n\theta&i\sin n\theta\\i\sin n\theta&\cos n\theta\end{bmatrix}$ because $i^2=-1$.
solution: (D) $a^2-c^2=\cos^25\theta+\sin^25\theta=1$: true. Hence the statement that is not true is (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\det A^5=(\det A)^5=1$ and the symmetry $a=d,\ b=c$ forced by $A=\cos\theta\,I+i\sin\theta\,J$.
solution: $A=\cos\theta\,I+i\sin\theta\,J$ with $J=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$; every power of $A$ is of the form $pI+qJ$, so $A^5$ has $a=d$ and $b=c$.
Also $a^2-d^2=0$ and $a^2-c^2=a^2-b^2=1$ follow at once, so (A) and (D) are true. Same answer (B).

useful_results: $\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&i\sin\theta\\i\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}^n=\begin{bmatrix}\cos n\theta&i\sin n\theta\\i\sin n\theta&\cos n\theta\end{bmatrix}$ (de Moivre, since $J^2=I$); likewise the rotation matrix $\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta\\-\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}^n$ has angle $n\theta$.
The family $pI+qJ$ with $J^2=I$ is closed under multiplication and commutative; $\det(pI+qJ)=p^2-q^2$.
$\det(A^n)=(\det A)^n$ gives invariants without computing $A^n$; here $\det A^5=1$.
Instance: $\cos^2\!\phi-i^2\sin^2\!\phi=1$ for every $\phi$, so any statement with $a^2-b^2$ and $a^2-c^2$ equal to $1$ is true.

concepts: Matrix equation $AX=B$ and determinant of a product
questions.question: Suppose the vectors $x_1,x_2,x_3$ are the solutions of the system of linear equations $Ax=b$ when the vector $b$ on the right side is equal to $b_1,b_2,b_3$ respectively. If $x_1=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{bmatrix},x_2=\begin{bmatrix}0\\2\\1\end{bmatrix},x_3=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{bmatrix},b_1=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{bmatrix},b_2=\begin{bmatrix}0\\2\\0\end{bmatrix}$ and $b_3=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\2\end{bmatrix}$, then the determinant of $A$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Put the solutions side by side: $A[x_1\ x_2\ x_3]=[b_1\ b_2\ b_3]$, i.e. $AX=B$, so $|A||X|=|B|$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Solve for $A$ itself, one column at a time, using the very simple $x_3=e_3$ and then $x_2$, $x_1$.
solution: $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\-1&1&0\\-1&-1&2\end{bmatrix}$ is lower triangular, so $|A|=1\cdot1\cdot2=2$. Same answer.

useful_results: Several solutions $Ax_k=b_k$ can be packed into one matrix equation $AX=B$; then $|A|=|B|/|X|$ (when $|X|\neq0$) and $A=BX^{-1}$.
The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries: no expansion needed.
$A(x_1\ x_2\ x_3)$ multiplies $A$ into each column separately, so the columns of $AX$ are $Ax_k$.
If $|X|=0$ the solutions are dependent and $|A|$ cannot be found this way.

concepts: Powers of a rotation matrix and determinant of $A+A^4$
questions.question: Let $\theta=\dfrac\pi5$ and $A=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta\\-\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}$. If $B=A+A^4$, then $\det(B)$:
questions.key_idea: Factor $B=A(I+A^3)$; $|A|=1$ and $A^3$ is the rotation by $3\theta$, so $|B|=2+2\cos3\theta$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Treat the rotation matrix as the complex number $z=e^{-i\theta}$: $\det$ of the matrix of $w$ is $|w|^2$.
solution: The matrices $\begin{bmatrix}p&q\\-q&p\end{bmatrix}$ multiply like complex numbers $p-iq$ and have determinant $p^2+q^2=|p-iq|^2$.
$\sin^236^\circ=\dfrac{1-\cos72^\circ}2=\dfrac{1-\frac{\sqrt5-1}4}2=\dfrac{5-\sqrt5}8$, so $|B|=\dfrac{5-\sqrt5}2\approx1.38$ and $|A|=1$ gives the same $|B|$. In $(1,2)$: same answer.

useful_results: $\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta\\-\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}^n$ is the same matrix with angle $n\theta$; rotation matrices commute and have determinant $1$.
For $M=\begin{bmatrix}p&q\\-q&p\end{bmatrix}$: $\det M=p^2+q^2$; $\det(I+R_\phi)=2+2\cos\phi=4\cos^2(\phi/2)$.
Exact values: $\sin18^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt5-1}4$, $\cos36^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt5+1}4$, $\cos72^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt5-1}4$.
Factor out the common matrix power first: $A+A^4=A(I+A^3)$ turns a sum into a product, so determinants multiply.

concepts: Symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices; solutions of a homogeneous system
questions.question: Let $A$ and $B$ be $3\times3$ real matrices such that $A$ is symmetric and $B$ is skew-symmetric. Then the system of linear equations $(A^2B^2-B^2A^2)X=O$, where $X$ is a $3\times1$ column matrix of unknown variables and $O$ is a $3\times1$ null matrix, has:
questions.key_idea: $A^2B^2-B^2A^2$ is skew-symmetric of odd order $3$, so its determinant is $0$.
solution: A skew-symmetric matrix of order $3$ has $\det=0$ (since $|S|=|S^T|=|-S|=-|S|$).
$\Rightarrow|A^2B^2-B^2A^2|=0$, so the homogeneous system has non-trivial solutions: infinitely many solutions, option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: A $3\times3$ skew-symmetric matrix is $K v=w\times v$ for a fixed vector $w$, so $w$ itself solves $KX=0$.
solution: Let $K=A^2B^2-B^2A^2$; it is skew-symmetric (shown by taking the transpose).
Every real skew-symmetric $3\times3$ matrix has the form $K=\begin{bmatrix}0&-w_3&w_2\\w_3&0&-w_1\\-w_2&w_1&0\end{bmatrix}$, and $Kv=w\times v$ for all $v$.
Then $Kw=w\times w=0$: the vector $w$ is a solution.
If $w\neq0$, every multiple $tw$ is also a solution; if $w=0$ then $K=O$ and every $X$ is a solution. Either way there are infinitely many solutions. Same answer (C).

useful_results: Odd-order skew-symmetric matrices are singular; even-order ones need not be (e.g. $\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}$).
The commutator $PQ-QP$ of two symmetric matrices is skew-symmetric, and of a symmetric and a skew matrix it is symmetric (check: transpose and swap).
Even powers of a skew-symmetric matrix are symmetric; odd powers are skew-symmetric.
A homogeneous system $MX=O$ has non-trivial (infinitely many) solutions exactly when $|M|=0$; it never has 'no solution' or 'exactly two'.

concepts: Matrix equations and inverse of a $2\times2$ matrix; trigonometric half-angle
questions.question: If $A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-\tan\left(\frac\theta2\right)\\\tan\left(\frac\theta2\right)&0\end{bmatrix}$ and $(I_2+A)(I_2-A)^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}a&-b\\b&a\end{bmatrix}$, then $13(a^2+b^2)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Multiply by $(I-A)$ to remove the inverse and compare entries; the sums of squares of two rows collapse to $a^2+b^2=1$.
useful_results: Cayley transform: if $A$ is skew-symmetric (and $I-A$ invertible) then $(I+A)(I-A)^{-1}$ is orthogonal with determinant $1$.
For the matrix $\begin{bmatrix}a&-b\\b&a\end{bmatrix}$ the determinant is $a^2+b^2$, so taking determinants of a matrix equation often gives $a^2+b^2$ in one line.
$I\pm A$ commute with each other (both are polynomials in $A$), so $(I+A)(I-A)^{-1}=(I-A)^{-1}(I+A)$.
Instance: with $t=\tan\frac\theta2$, $(I+A)(I-A)^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}$ (the half-angle formulas $\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2},\frac{2t}{1+t^2}$).

concepts: Symmetric matrices of order 2 and trace of $A^2$
questions.question: Let $A$ be a symmetric matrix of order $2$ with integer entries. If the sum of the diagonal elements of $A^2$ is $1$, then the possible number of such matrices is:
questions.key_idea: For $A=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{bmatrix}$, $\operatorname{tr}(A^2)=a^2+2b^2+c^2$; with integer entries this equals $1$ only if $b=0$.
useful_results: $\operatorname{tr}(A^TA)$ is the sum of squares of all entries; for symmetric $A$, $\operatorname{tr}(A^2)=\sum a_{ij}^2$, so an off-diagonal entry is counted twice.
Integer solutions of $a^2+2b^2+c^2=1$: the sum of non-negative integer squares equal to $1$ means exactly one square is $1$ and the rest $0$; a $b$ entry costs $2$, so it is excluded.

For a $2\times2$ symmetric matrix with $\operatorname{tr}A^2=m$ the count of integer matrices is the number of integer points on the ellipsoid $a^2+2b^2+c^2=m$; here $m=1$ gives $4$ (the points $(\pm1,0,0),(0,0,\pm1)$).
Count carefully with signs: each non-zero entry contributes a factor $2$ for $\pm$.

concepts: Determinant of a matrix expression and trigonometric equation
questions.question: If $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sin\alpha\\\sin\alpha&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\det\left(A^2-\dfrac12I\right)=0$, then a possible value of $\alpha$ is:
questions.key_idea: $A^2=\sin^2\alpha\cdot I$ is scalar, so $\det\left(A^2-\tfrac12I\right)=\left(\sin^2\alpha-\tfrac12\right)^2$.
solution: $\sin\alpha=\dfrac1{\sqrt2}$ or $\sin\alpha=-\dfrac1{\sqrt2}$; the second gives $\alpha=-\dfrac\pi4,\dfrac{5\pi}4,\ldots$, none of which is among the options.
questions.correction_note: The PDF dismisses $\sin\alpha=-1/\sqrt2$ as 'Rejected' (taking $\alpha\in[0,\pi/2]$, which the question never states). That value also satisfies the equation; it simply gives no option. The answer $\pi/4$ is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eigenvalues of $A$ are $\pm\sin\alpha$, so $\det(A^2-\tfrac12I)=\prod(\lambda^2-\tfrac12)$; then test the four options.
solution: $A^2-\tfrac12I$ has eigenvalues $\lambda^2-\tfrac12=\sin^2\alpha-\tfrac12$ (twice), so the determinant is $\left(\sin^2\alpha-\tfrac12\right)^2$.

useful_results: For $\begin{pmatrix}0&p\\p&0\end{pmatrix}$ the square is $p^2I$; for $\begin{pmatrix}0&p\\q&0\end{pmatrix}$ the square is $pq\,I$.
If $M=kI$ then $\det(M-cI)=(k-c)^n$ for an $n\times n$ matrix: zero exactly when $k=c$.
$\det(f(A))=\prod f(\lambda_i)$ over the eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ of $A$ (for a polynomial $f$).
When the options are given, substituting them in $\sin^2\alpha=\tfrac12$ is the fastest check: only $\alpha=\pi/4$ among the standard angles.

concepts: Powers of a matrix and consistency of a linear system
questions.question: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}i&-i\\-i&i\end{bmatrix}$, $i=\sqrt{-1}$. Then the system of linear equations $A^8\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8\\64\end{bmatrix}$ has:
questions.key_idea: $A^8$ has proportional rows ($R_2=-R_1$) but the right side is not in the same ratio, so the system is inconsistent.
solution: Adding, $0=72$, which is impossible: the system has no solution.
questions.correction_note: In the PDF's first line the first factor of $AA$ is printed as $\begin{bmatrix}i&i\\-i&i\end{bmatrix}$ (top-right entry $i$); $A$ has $-i$ there. With the correct factor the product $\begin{bmatrix}-2&2\\2&-2\end{bmatrix}$ is what the PDF shows, so every later line and the answer are unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: $A=iN$ with $N=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}$ and $N^2=2N$, so $A^8=i^8N^8=2^7N$ in one step.
solution: The system is $128(x-y)=8$ and $-128(x-y)=64$, i.e. $x-y=\tfrac1{16}$ and $x-y=-\tfrac12$.
Contradictory, so there is no solution. Same answer.

useful_results: A rank-one matrix $N=uv^T$ satisfies $N^2=(v^Tu)N$, so $N^k=(v^Tu)^{k-1}N$; here $u=(1,-1)^T$, $v=(1,-1)^T$, $v^Tu=2$.

System $\begin{bmatrix}p&q\\kp&kq\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}r\\s\end{bmatrix}$ is consistent iff $s=kr$ (then infinitely many solutions), otherwise inconsistent; $|M|=0$ alone does not give infinitely many.
If $|A^8|=|A|^8=0$ then the system $A^8x=b$ has either no solution or infinitely many; compare the right side with the row dependency to decide.
Instance: rows of $A^8$ satisfy $R_1+R_2=0$, so a solution needs $8+64=0$; it fails.

concepts: Algebra of matrices: inverse and commutativity
questions.question: If $A$ and $B$ are two non-zero $n\times n$ matrices such that $A^2+B=A^2B$, then:
questions.key_idea: $A^2+B=A^2B\iff(A^2-I)(B-I)=I$, so the two factors are inverses of each other and therefore commute.
solution: Since $A^2+B=A^2B$, we get $A^2B=BA^2$, so (A) is correct.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's fourth line reads $A^2B(B-I)^{-1}$; this is a garbled version of $A^2=B(B-I)^{-1}$ (multiply $A^2(B-I)=B$ on the right by $(B-I)^{-1}$). As printed it is not a valid step. The PDF also does not say why $(B-I)^{-1}$ exists and equals $A^2-I$ (it follows from line $(1)$); both are added. The final result is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: $B-I=(A^2-I)^{-1}$, so $B=I+(A^2-I)^{-1}$ is a function of $A^2$ and therefore commutes with $A^2$.
solution: As above, $(A^2-I)(B-I)=I$, so $A^2-I$ is invertible and $B-I=(A^2-I)^{-1}$.
$A^2$ commutes with $A^2-I$, hence with its inverse (if $XY=YX$ and $X$ is invertible then $X^{-1}Y=YX^{-1}$) and with $I$.

useful_results: Factorisation trick: $XY-X-Y=0\iff(X-I)(Y-I)=I$ for matrices as for numbers; here $X=A^2$, $Y=B$.
In a finite-dimensional matrix ring, $XY=I\Rightarrow YX=I$: one-sided inverses are two-sided, so $(A^2-I)(B-I)=I\Rightarrow(B-I)(A^2-I)=I$.
Anything that is a rational function of $A$ (polynomials and inverses of polynomials in $A$) commutes with $A$.
The relation is symmetric in the roles: from $(B-I)(A^2-I)=I$ one gets $BA^2=A^2+B$ directly.

concepts: Singular matrix, root of a quadratic and algebraic identities
questions.question: Let $\alpha$ be a root of the equation $(a-c)x^2+(b-a)x+(c-b)=0$ where $a,b,c$ are distinct real numbers such that the matrix $\begin{bmatrix}\alpha^2&\alpha&1\\1&1&1\\a&b&c\end{bmatrix}$ is singular. Then the value of $\dfrac{(a-c)^2}{(b-a)(c-b)}+\dfrac{(b-a)^2}{(a-c)(c-b)}+\dfrac{(c-b)^2}{(a-c)(b-a)}$ is:
questions.key_idea: With $x=a-b,\ y=b-c,\ z=c-a$ (so $x+y+z=0$) the sum is $\dfrac{x^3+y^3+z^3}{xyz}=3$; the singular-matrix condition is not even needed.
solution: The coefficients of this quadratic add up to $0$ and so do those of the given one, so $\alpha=1$ satisfies both: the matrix is singular when $\alpha=1$.
The expression becomes $\dfrac{z^2}{xy}+\dfrac{x^2}{yz}+\dfrac{y^2}{zx}=\dfrac{z^3+x^3+y^3}{xyz}$ (as the PDF writes, with numerator $(a-b)^3+(b-c)^3+(c-a)^3$).
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the combined numerator as $(a-b)^3+(b-c)^3+(c-a)^3$ over $(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$ (and a denominator $(b-a)(c-b)(a-c)$ in the intermediate line) without showing the sign handling; the value $3$ is correct. The sign handling is added (terms are $z^2/xy,\ x^2/yz,\ y^2/zx$), and the remark that the result is independent of $\alpha$. Nothing else changed.

alternate_solutions.idea: The options are constants, so the value cannot depend on $a,b,c$: substitute convenient distinct numbers.
solution: The expression is the same for every admissible $a,b,c$ (and $\alpha=1$ always makes the matrix singular), so take $a=0,b=1,c=3$.

useful_results: If $x+y+z=0$ then $x^3+y^3+z^3=3xyz$; hence for $x=a-b$, $y=b-c$, $z=c-a$: $(a-b)^3+(b-c)^3+(c-a)^3=3(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$.
For $px^2+qx+r=0$ with $p+q+r=0$, $x=1$ is a root; the other root is $r/p$.
The determinant $\begin{vmatrix}\alpha^2&\alpha&1\\1&1&1\\a&b&c\end{vmatrix}$ vanishes at $\alpha=1$ for every $a,b,c$ (rows 1 and 2 become equal).
When an answer must be a constant, a numerical substitution of simple distinct values is a valid and fast check.

concepts: Permutations and counting of 0-1 matrices
questions.question: The number of square matrices of order $5$ with entries from the set $\{0,1\}$, such that the sum of all the elements in each row is $1$ and the sum of all the elements in each column is also $1$, is:
questions.key_idea: Exactly one $1$ in each row and each column means a permutation matrix: place the $1$s row by row, one fewer free column each time.
solution: Each row and each column must contain exactly one $1$ (the other entries are $0$).
Row 1: the $1$ can go in any of $5$ columns, which then has no room for another $1$.
Row 3: $3$ ways; row 4: $2$ ways; row 5: $1$ way.
questions.correction_note: In the PDF's alternate layout the number of ways written beside rows 1-5 is '5, 4, 3, 4, 1'; the fourth should be $2$ (the product $5\cdot4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1=120$ is what the PDF finally uses). Corrected; the answer is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Rows give a function $f:\{1..5\}\to\{1..5\}$; column sums $1$ means $f$ is a bijection, counted by inclusion-exclusion on surjections.
solution: A matrix with every row sum $1$ is a function $f$ (row $\to$ column of its $1$): $5^5=3125$ such matrices.
Every column sum $1$ means each column is hit exactly once, i.e. $f$ is onto (and, 5 rows into 5 columns, a bijection).

useful_results: $n\times n$ 0-1 matrices with every row sum and column sum equal to $1$ are exactly the permutation matrices; there are $n!$.
Matrices with every row sum $1$ (columns free) number $n^n$; with row sums $1$ and column sums $\le1$ you again get $n!$.
Onto functions from an $n$-set to an $n$-set number $n!$: $\sum_k(-1)^k\binom nk(n-k)^n=n!$ (an identity).
Counting rule: place items row by row, and each placement removes one column from the later rows (multiplication principle).

concepts: Determinants with logarithmic entries
Adjoint of a matrix
questions.question: Let $x,y,z>1$ and $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&\log_xy&\log_xz\\\log_yx&2&\log_yz\\\log_zx&\log_zy&3\end{bmatrix}$. Then $|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A^2)|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Convert every entry to $\log$ ratios and pull $\log x,\log y,\log z$ out of rows/columns to get $|A|=\begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\1&2&1\\1&1&3\end{vmatrix}=2$.
solution: $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&\frac{\log y}{\log x}&\frac{\log z}{\log x}\\\frac{\log x}{\log y}&2&\frac{\log z}{\log y}\\\frac{\log x}{\log z}&\frac{\log y}{\log z}&3\end{bmatrix}$.
$|A|=\dfrac1{\log x\log y\log z}\begin{vmatrix}\log x&\log y&\log z\\\log x&2\log y&\log z\\\log x&\log y&3\log z\end{vmatrix}$ (rows $1,2,3$ multiplied by $\log x,\log y,\log z$).
Take $\log x,\log y,\log z$ out of columns $1,2,3$: $|A|=\begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\1&2&1\\1&1&3\end{vmatrix}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $A=D^{-1}KD$ with $D=\operatorname{diag}(\log x,\log y,\log z)$: similar matrices have equal determinants; and $\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}M)=|M|M$ for $3\times3$.
solution: For a $3\times3$ matrix $M$, $\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}M)=|M|^{3-2}M=|M|M$; so with $M=A^2$ ($|M|=4$), $|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}M)|=|M|^3|M|=|M|^4=4^4=2^8$. Same answer.

useful_results: $\log_ab=\dfrac{\log b}{\log a}$, so a matrix with entries $\log_{a_i}a_j$ off the diagonal is $D^{-1}KD$ and has determinant $|K|$.
Conjugation by a diagonal matrix $D^{-1}KD$ multiplies $K_{ij}$ by $d_j/d_i$ and leaves the diagonal and $|K|$ unchanged.
$|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}M)|=|M|^{(n-1)^2}$ and $\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}M)=|M|^{n-2}M$.
Check on a small case: $M=2I_3$, $\operatorname{adj}M=4I$, $\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}M)=16I$, determinant $4096=8^4=|M|^4$.

concepts: Orthogonal matrices and powers of a unipotent matrix
questions.question: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}\frac1{\sqrt{10}}&\frac3{\sqrt{10}}\\-\frac3{\sqrt{10}}&\frac1{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{bmatrix}1&-i\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$, where $i=\sqrt{-1}$. If $M=A^TBA$, then the inverse of the matrix $AM^{2023}A^T$ is
questions.key_idea: $AA^T=I$, so $AM^nA^T=(AMA^T)^n=B^n$; then $B^n$ just adds $-i$ to the corner each time.

alternate_solutions.idea: $B=I+N$ with $N^2=0$, so $B^n=I+nN$ by the binomial theorem and $B^{-n}=I-nN$; conjugation by $A$ is multiplicative.
solution: $A^TA=I$ too, so $X\mapsto AXA^T$ preserves products: $AM^nA^T=(AMA^T)^n$, and $AMA^T=AA^TBAA^T=B$.

useful_results: If $A$ is orthogonal ($AA^T=I$) then $(A^TBA)^n=A^TB^nA$: orthogonal conjugation commutes with taking powers.
A matrix $I+N$ with $N^2=0$ satisfies $(I+N)^n=I+nN$ for every integer $n$ (including negative: $(I+N)^{-1}=I-N$).
$\begin{bmatrix}1&c\\0&1\end{bmatrix}^n=\begin{bmatrix}1&nc\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$, and its inverse is $\begin{bmatrix}1&-c\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$.
A matrix $\frac1{\sqrt{p^2+q^2}}\begin{bmatrix}p&q\\-q&p\end{bmatrix}$ is always orthogonal (a rotation matrix); here $(p,q)=(1,3)$.

concepts: Symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices
questions.question: Let $A,B,C$ be $3\times3$ matrices such that $A$ is symmetric and $B$ and $C$ are skew-symmetric. Consider the statements (S1) $A^{13}B^{26}-B^{26}A^{13}$ is symmetric; (S2) $A^{26}C^{13}-C^{13}A^{26}$ is symmetric. Then
options: Both S1 and S2 are true
Both S1 and S2 are false
questions.key_idea: Transpose reverses products; odd powers of a skew matrix stay skew, even powers become symmetric.
solution: $=-(A^{13}B^{26}-B^{26}A^{13})$, so S1's matrix is skew-symmetric (not symmetric in general): S1 is false.
$=A^{26}C^{13}-C^{13}A^{26}$, so it is symmetric: S2 is true.
Hence S2 is true and S1 is false: option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Sign rule for commutators: $[U,V]^T=-\varepsilon_U\varepsilon_V[U,V]$ where $\varepsilon=\pm1$ marks symmetric or skew.
solution: So $UV-VU$ is symmetric iff $\varepsilon_U\varepsilon_V=-1$ (one symmetric, one skew), and skew iff $\varepsilon_U\varepsilon_V=+1$.
Types of the powers: $A^{13}$ and $A^{26}$ are symmetric ($\varepsilon=+1$); $B^{26}$ is symmetric ($(-1)^{26}=+1$); $C^{13}$ is skew ($(-1)^{13}=-1$).
S1: $\varepsilon_{A^{13}}\varepsilon_{B^{26}}=(+1)(+1)=+1$, so the commutator is skew-symmetric: S1 is false (it is not symmetric unless it is zero).
S2: $\varepsilon_{A^{26}}\varepsilon_{C^{13}}=(+1)(-1)=-1$, so the commutator is symmetric: S2 true. Same answer (D).

useful_results: $(X^n)^T=(X^T)^n$; for a skew matrix $S$, $(S^n)^T=(-1)^nS^n$: even powers symmetric, odd powers skew.
Commutator $[U,V]=UV-VU$ is symmetric when one of $U,V$ is symmetric and the other skew; it is skew when both are symmetric or both skew.
Anti-commutator $UV+VU$ has the opposite behaviour: symmetric when both are of the same type.

Check: $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}$, $C=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}$: $AC-CA=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-2&0\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0&2\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}$, symmetric.

concepts: Polynomial relations in a matrix (Cayley-Hamilton type reduction)
questions.question: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be real numbers. Consider a $3\times3$ matrix $A$ such that $A^2=3A+\alpha I$. If $A^4=21A+\beta I$, then
questions.key_idea: Reduce $A^3$ and $A^4$ to the form $pA+qI$ with $A^2=3A+\alpha I$ and compare coefficients of $A$ and $I$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Treat the relation as a quadratic with roots $r,s$ ($r+s=3$, $rs=-\alpha$); both roots satisfy $\lambda^4=21\lambda+\beta$, so subtract.
solution: $\lambda=r,s$ are roots of $\lambda^2-3\lambda-\alpha=0$, so $r+s=3$, $rs=-\alpha$; each root satisfies $\lambda^4=21\lambda+\beta$.

useful_results: If $A^2=pA+qI$ then every power is $A^n=a_nA+b_nI$ with $a_{n+1}=pa_n+b_n$, $b_{n+1}=qa_n$ (reduce one power at a time).
$A^3=(p^2+q)A+pqI$ and $A^4=(p^3+2pq)A+(p^2q+q^2)I$ for $A^2=pA+qI$; here $p=3,q=\alpha$ gives $27+6\alpha$ and $9\alpha+\alpha^2$.
The same relation holds for every eigenvalue of $A$, so polynomial relations among matrix powers can be solved as scalar equations on eigenvalues.

Instance: with $\alpha=-1$, $A^2=3A-I$, $A^4=21A-8I$ (check on $A=\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$: $A^2=\begin{bmatrix}8&-3\\3&-1\end{bmatrix}=3A-I$, $A^4=\begin{bmatrix}55&-21\\21&-8\end{bmatrix}=21A-8I$).
